inputs.jd_text:
Associate Product Manager - Merchant Payments
Paynest (Bengaluru)

Paynest is a payments company serving 4 lakh small merchants across India with UPI QR, soundboxes and working-capital loans.

What you'll do
- Own a part of the merchant app (onboarding, settlements or the loans journey) end to end
- Talk to merchants regularly, especially in tier-2 and tier-3 cities, and turn what you learn into product decisions
- Define success metrics, run experiments and make prioritisation calls with engineering and design
- Work with risk, credit and operations teams on launches

What we're looking for
- MBA from a top institute; 2+ years of prior work experience preferred (engineering background a plus)
- Strong product sense and comfort with data (SQL a plus)
- Clear communication with both merchants and engineers
- Hindi or a regional language is a plus

transcript.text: Hi Arjun, thanks for making the time. I'm on the team hiring for the Associate Product Manager - Merchant Payments role at Paynest. Over the next 15 minutes or so I'd like to go into your experience, and you'll have time for questions at the end. What have you been working on or learning lately at IIM Bangalore?
transcript.why: This was a warm-up question to help you settle in. It isn't part of the feedback.

transcript.text: um sure sir thanks for having me so at IIM Bangalore recently we have been doing a lot of case-based learning actually and like in the past term I got really interested in courses like marketing and product management and also a bit of fintech so we worked in teams quite a lot like solving business problems so mostly what I’ve been focusing on is improving how I approach new problem statements and come up with structured solutions and I’ve also been learning about user research a bit especially because of my internship so I try to talk to users and validate assumptions apart from academics I’ve also been quite involved in the product management club where we discuss trends and do mock PM interviews so um yeah that’s mostly what I’m doing right now
Thanks. Walk me through your career so far, from Infosys through your MBA and summer at Swiggy.
transcript.why: This opening question was simply to understand what you have been focused on recently before discussing your experience.

transcript.text: okay sir so basically after my BTech from NIT Calicut I joined Infosys as a systems engineer and I worked there for three years so most of my work was for a European bank where our team was building backend APIs for their loan platform um I worked quite a lot on improving the API performance and we also tried to make the codebase better for new people joining so I mentored a few freshers also then after Infosys I joined IIM Bangalore for my MBA and here I started focusing more on product management so for my summer internship I worked at Swiggy Instamart as a product intern there I worked on features like the frequently bought together widget and we did quite a bit of user research so yeah after all that experience I feel I want to go deeper into product roles now
I see you owned a cart-page widget at Swiggy Instamart. What product decision were you responsible for there?
transcript.why: Your answer outlined your path through engineering, business school, and product work, so I moved to a specific product decision from your Swiggy internship.

transcript.text: um yes so actually I was mainly responsible for like deciding how the frequently bought together widget should look and what products to show in it so first we looked at the user journey on the cart page and we saw that people sometimes just checkout without exploring extra items so I worked with the design and analytics teams to shortlist ideas and like I coordinated the A/B experiment also so we had to take a call on how aggressive the recommendations should be when to show the widget and also which logic should power it so I discussed with the data team about the recommendation algorithm and also decided with my mentor which metrics to track we finally pushed it live to a small chunk of users and then improved it based on early results so yeah that was the main decision area for me
Which decision about the widget did you personally make and take forward?
transcript.why: You described several decisions made with design, analytics, data, and your mentor, so I asked which decision was personally yours.

transcript.text: um yeah so actually there was one point where we had to decide whether the widget should come up only if there are at least two items in the cart or even for a single item and this was like a bit debated in the team so I suggested we should try showing it even when there’s just one item in the cart because from some of our user calls we had feedback that people sometimes forget basics like bread or milk so by surfacing items earlier it might nudge them to add more so I convinced my mentor and the analytics person to test both and we updated the logic to actually show it in both cases and that version ended up performing a bit better in terms of extra items added so that was the decision I personally pushed for
You mentioned the version performed better for extra items added. How was the 3.4% lift in average order value measured?
transcript.why: You described the decision you personally pushed forward and said it performed better. I asked how the reported lift was measured and what comparison established it.

transcript.text: um so actually for that we did an A/B test where like eight percent of the Instamart traffic got the new widget version and the rest stayed on the old version so the analytics team tracked the average order value for users in both groups and compared them after a couple of weeks and we saw that the group with the updated widget had a 3.4 percent higher order value on average so that’s what we reported as the lift um the numbers were all pulled from Swiggy’s dashboards so that’s how we measured it actually
At Infosys, you improved the loan platform's API speed. What led you to investigate caching?
transcript.why: Your answer clarified how the lift was compared between the updated and old widget groups and where the figures came from. I’m moving to another concrete project to understand your technical decision-making.

transcript.text: so actually what happened is like our team started getting complaints from the client that the API to fetch credit info was becoming slow especially during peak times and users were waiting quite a bit we also saw a spike in latency metrics on the monitoring tool so first we tried to check if there were any obvious issues or slow queries but most things were fine then we realised that the credit bureau lookup called an external service every single time and that backend was sometimes slow so after discussing with my lead and like looking at the patterns we figured that for some users the data doesn’t change often so caching would help I proposed using Redis and did a small proof of concept and after that we implemented it and saw the latency improve lots so yeah that’s how we came to caching
What made Redis suitable for caching those credit-bureau lookups in your design?
transcript.why: You described the external lookup and your proof of concept, so I asked what made Redis suitable for that specific access pattern.

transcript.text: um so actually we went with Redis mainly because it’s really fast for reading and writing data from memory and that was important since we needed the API response times to drop quickly also Redis supports things like key expiry so we could easily set a short TTL for the cache and not worry about serving outdated credit data plus in our team some folks had used Redis before so we already had some idea about how to set it up with Spring Boot and integrate it with our service also given the volume of our requests and the need for quick failover Redis seemed quite a good fit compared to like database-level caching so yeah that’s why we thought Redis made sense for our use case
How did you measure the change from 1.8 seconds to 600 milliseconds at p95?
transcript.why: You explained why Redis suited the lookup workload, but not how the latency improvement was measured. I asked about the basis for the two p95 figures.

transcript.text: um so basically we were using some monitoring tools like Grafana and Prometheus in our project so they were tracking the response times for all the API calls in real time and we had dashboards showing the p95 latency numbers so before we put the cache we saw that the p95—which is like the 95th percentile—was hovering around 1.8 seconds during busy periods after we added Redis and rolled it out in production we kept monitoring the same dashboard and saw that over the next week or so the p95 dropped to around 600 milliseconds consistently so we mostly relied on those metrics from the dashboard to measure the improvement and just checked over a few days that things stayed stable
Thanks. Let’s turn to merchant onboarding. How would you decide whether an onboarding change is helping merchants in tier-2 cities?
transcript.why: I asked how the latency change was measured because the resume included specific before-and-after p95 figures. Your answer identified the monitoring tools, comparison period, and how the result was tracked after launch.

Associate Product Manager - Merchant Payments
Paynest (Bengaluru)

Paynest is a payments company serving 4 lakh small merchants across India with UPI QR, soundboxes and working-capital loans.

What you'll do
- Own a part of the merchant app (onboarding, settlements or the loans journey) end to end
- Talk to merchants regularly, especially in tier-2 and tier-3 cities, and turn what you learn into product decisions
- Define success metrics, run experiments and make prioritisation calls with engineering and design
- Work with risk, credit and operations teams on launches

What we're looking for
- MBA from a top institute; 2+ years of prior work experience preferred (engineering background a plus)
- Strong product sense and comfort with data (SQL a plus)
- Clear communication with both merchants and engineers
- Hindi or a regional language is a plus
